title: Mouth ulcers on methotrexate taken daily — prioritise the dangerous decision

blocks.text: Mouth ulcers on methotrexate taken daily — prioritise the dangerous decision

AMaC MRCP PACES23 • Round 5 • R5-233 • Station 2: Consultation (acute presentation) • 20 minutes • Skills A–G (clinical examination as indicated) • 14 October 2026 • Unofficial educational marking descriptors

A 67-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis reports painful mouth ulcers and diarrhoea. Medicine reconciliation reveals they have taken methotrexate every morning for six days rather than once a week. Take a focused history, assess immediate safety and agree the initial management with the patient or caller.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK: Potentially severe low-dose methotrexate overdose from daily rather than weekly dosing with mucosal toxicity and possible marrow suppression, renal injury or sepsis.

TRAP: This is a potentially fatal medication error. Escalate immediately, document the actual regimen, apply duty of candour according to local policy, and investigate prescribing/dispensing/administration causes without blaming the patient.

rows: “I need to check whether you need urgent help.”

This is a potentially fatal medication error. Escalate immediately, document the actual regimen, apply duty of candour according to local policy, and investigate prescribing/dispensing/administration causes without blaming the patient.
“I’ll ask questions that distinguish the causes.”

Establish tablets and strength, exactly how many doses and dates, last dose, folic acid, renal function, interacting medicines, temperature, mouth pain, bleeding, breathlessness, urine output and who arranged the prescription.
“There is a concern that needs checking.”
Potentially severe low-dose methotrexate overdose from daily rather than weekly dosing with mucosal toxicity and possible marrow suppression, renal injury or sepsis.

Stop methotrexate, arrange emergency hospital evaluation with FBC/differential, renal and liver function, electrolytes and infection assessment. Contact toxicology and haematology/rheumatology urgently.
Treats daily methotrexate as a usual regimen for RA
Recognises potentially fatal inadvertent daily low-dose methotrexate overdose
Links mucositis and diarrhoea to toxicity and marrow suppression
Advises continuing methotrexate and routine appointment
Instructs no further methotrexate and arranges emergency hospital assessment
Confirms tablet strength, dose taken each day, number of days and last ingestion
Reviews interactions, renal function and folic acid use
Omits blood counts because ulcers are local
Urgently obtains FBC, U&E/eGFR, LFT and infection/sepsis assessment
Recognises evolving cytopenia may warrant serial monitoring
Treats with routine folic acid alone

Requests immediate specialist-directed folinic acid rescue and supportive management: calcium folinate (folinic acid) given promptly, e.g. 15 mg IV or oral every 6 hours, with dosing and duration guided by TOXBASE or poisons-centre and haematology advice and by the blood count and mucositis (serum methotrexate levels guide high-dose protocols, not this scenario)
Coordinates infection control, fluids and additional antidotal decisions with toxicology
Responds non-judgementally, records error and explains once-weekly dosing
Arranges medicines reconciliation, incident reporting and patient/carer safety advice

blocks.text: Patient is embarrassed: “I followed the label—I thought it was daily.” Respond respectfully and avoid blame. Give only history elicited by candidate; do not volunteer the diagnosis or investigation results.

Immediate action — Instructs no further methotrexate and arranges emergency hospital assessment. Urgently alerts acute medicine/haematology/toxicology teams

THINK: Potentially severe low-dose methotrexate overdose from daily rather than weekly dosing with mucosal toxicity and possible marrow suppression, renal injury or sepsis. SAY: explain uncertainty clearly. DO: Stop methotrexate, arrange emergency hospital evaluation with FBC/differential, renal and liver function, electrolytes and infection assessment. Contact toxicology and haematology/rheumatology urgently. NUMBERS: 20-minute consultation. TRAP: This is a potentially fatal medication error. Escalate immediately, document the actual regimen, apply duty of candour according to local policy, and investigate prescribing/dispensing/administration causes without blaming the patient. FINISH: Begin specialist-directed folinic acid (calcium folinate/leucovorin) rescue promptly, with supportive care and antimicrobial/neutropenic sepsis treatment if needed; assess renal impairment and interacting drugs. Do not substitute routine folic acid for antidotal folinic acid.
